scenarios.description: Chest CT + clinical nomogram for COVID-19 pneumonia progression (Nat Commun 2020) lacks validation in any independent population beyond the development site.
scenarios.query_text: This COVID-19 progression nomogram was built and tested entirely within one hospital's CT cohort. Reviewers should ask whether discrimination and calibration hold up on patients from a different center before any clinical reading.

scenarios.description: Five-year osteoarthritis risk model (UK Biobank, Nat Commun 2024) is 'validated' only via an internal UKB subsample, never on a separate cohort.
scenarios.query_text: Splitting UK Biobank into train and test is not external validation. A held-out UKB sample shares the same recruitment biases as the development set, so an independent OA cohort is required before generalizable risk claims.

scenarios.description: HIV mortality plasma proteomics panel (Nat Commun 2025) shows a large unexplained sensitivity drop on a small 127-sample validation cohort, with key supplementary missing.
scenarios.query_text: Sensitivity collapses from the training cohort to a 127-patient validation set with no clear explanation. Either the validation cohort is too small to draw conclusions or there is a distribution shift the authors have not characterized.

scenarios.description: Prehospital trauma mortality model (Nat Commun 2025) trained in South Korea, externally tested only at one Australian center; no US or European EMS data.
scenarios.query_text: One external Australian site is a start, but EMS protocols, triage thresholds, and trauma case mix vary widely between healthcare systems. Generalizability claims need testing in US or European EMS cohorts before broad deployment.

scenarios.description: TransformEHR self-harm prediction (Nat Commun 2023) reports PPV of 1.7% yet claims clinical utility, which would mean 98% of triggered interventions go to non-harming patients.
scenarios.query_text: At a PPV under 2%, nearly every alert is a false positive. The authors' claim that an 8.45% PPV minimizes resource cost needs an actual decision analysis or net benefit calculation, not assertion.

scenarios.description: Multimodal ultrasound ovarian cancer model (Nat Commun 2024) demonstrates discrimination mainly on clinically obvious cases (huge CA125, massive ascites), not the hard cases that matter at decision time.
scenarios.query_text: A model that flags ovarian cancer in patients with massive ascites or CA125 above 10,000 adds little to clinical workflow. The case for utility rests on the small-mass, normal-CA125 subgroup where physicians actually need help, and that subgroup is not evaluated.

scenarios.description: Cervical cancer WSI deep learning model (Nat Commun 2021) is evaluated as a primary screen, but with HPV testing now the first-line screen, the relevant deployment subgroup (HPV-positive women) is not assessed.
scenarios.query_text: Screening guidelines have shifted toward HPV testing first, so the practically relevant question is how the cytology AI performs on HPV-positive women. The current evaluation treats the model as a primary screen and skips the subgroup where it would actually be used.

scenarios.description: Deep learning early-response model for metastatic colorectal cancer (Nat Commun 2021) is not benchmarked against nested clinical baselines (RECIST, ETS) to show added prognostic value.
scenarios.query_text: A sophisticated DL signature only matters if it beats clinically available predictors. Authors should fit nested models adding RECIST and early tumor shrinkage stepwise and quantify how much variance in overall survival the DL features contribute beyond standard features.

scenarios.description: COVID-19 severity progression model based on extensive immunophenotyping (Nat Commun 2022) is claimed to be applicable in clinic, but the assay turnaround is incompatible with rapid deterioration.
scenarios.query_text: Patients in this cohort decompensate within days, while the immunophenotyping panel takes much longer to run and is resource-intensive. The 'applied rapidly in clinic' framing should be revised or supported with realistic turnaround and cost data.

scenarios.description: Breast cancer radiogenomic prognostic signature (Nat Commun 2020) is not compared against established clinical signatures (MammaPrint, OncotypeDX) to demonstrate added prognostic value.
scenarios.query_text: Several gene-expression signatures are already in routine use for breast cancer prognostication. The new radiogenomic biomarker needs head-to-head and additive analyses against MammaPrint and OncotypeDX before any claim of clinical contribution.

scenarios.query_text: A 25% bioinformatic holdout is not an external cohort. For a pediatric TB classifier the meaningful test is performance on independent samples from a different country and within HIV-positive and age subgroups, none of which is reported.

scenarios.description: Burdensome multi-device wearable protocol with no reporting of adherence, completion, or dropout — reporting gap that undermines feasibility claims.
scenarios.query_text: Each participant was asked to wear four accelerometers for a week, yet the manuscript reports no adherence rate, no wear-time completion, and no dropout figures — patient-burden metrics are essential here.

scenarios.description: Prospective deployment paper omits clinician training, workflow integration, and alert-fatigue handling — TRIPOD+AI deployment-reporting failure.
scenarios.query_text: The paper never explains what physicians were told before the trial, how the risk score appeared inside their workflow, what training they received, or how alert fatigue was monitored — all standard items for an implementation study.

scenarios.description: Manuscript reports conflicting cutoffs, p-values, and survival-curve numbers between text, tables, and figures — reporting accuracy / data-integrity issue.
scenarios.query_text: The training-set cutoff differs from what is applied at validation, the TCGA median is yet another number, the headline p-value is given as 0.004 in one place and 0.042 in another (and stated as <0.001 in the abstract), and the at-risk table does not match the Kaplan-Meier plot.

scenarios.description: UK Biobank cancer-outcome study omits the data field used for case ascertainment and the censoring date — basic reporting completeness failure.
scenarios.query_text: Which UK Biobank field was used to identify cancer cases, and what is the end-of-follow-up date applied here? Both are missing, and they matter because the cancer registry is refreshed periodically.

scenarios.description: Prognostic model submission lacks a TRIPOD statement / checklist and does not justify the choice of all-cause mortality endpoint or the prediction horizon.
scenarios.query_text: A TRIPOD statement and completed checklist should accompany this prognostic model. Authors should also defend their use of all-cause rather than cause-specific mortality and state the exact survival horizon being predicted.

scenarios.description: Multi-center IVF study reports only pooled metrics with no per-clinic descriptives or reclassification — center-level reporting failure that hides heterogeneity.
scenarios.query_text: Results pool six clinics together with no per-site AMH, age, or reclassification tables. Without per-clinic breakdowns it is impossible to evaluate center-specific performance claims.

scenarios.description: Released GNN repository omits tool version pins, input-format specification, and output-file documentation — reproducibility deficit despite code release.
scenarios.query_text: The AMR-GNN repository pins no version numbers, never describes the expected input format or how a user should prepare their data, and the output files are unannotated — anyone outside the original team cannot reproduce the pipeline.

scenarios.description: Authors release some code but restrict raw sequencing data — incomplete reproducibility package that blocks independent verification of figures and survival analysis.
scenarios.query_text: It is unclear whether the code and data needed to reproduce the figures and survival analyses are actually being shared. The raw targeted-sequencing reads from tumor and liquid biopsies should be deposited too, not just summary tables.

scenarios.description: Deep-learning paper omits loss function, optimizer, epochs, dev split, and image preprocessing while ensembling 20 randomly hyperparameterized models — opaque training pipeline.
scenarios.query_text: The deep-learning description does not state the loss function, optimizer, number of epochs, or development split, and the DICOM-to-PNG preprocessing (dimensions, cropping, augmentation) is entirely absent. On top of that, twenty models with random hyperparameters are ensembled without explaining how they are combined.

scenarios.description: Synthetic-data manuscript releases neither real source data, synthetic outputs, nor a public code repository — reproducibility triad failure.
scenarios.query_text: For a synthetic-data paper the bar is straightforward: are the real inputs available, are the synthetic outputs available, and is the code public? Here the answer to all three appears to be no, so the work cannot be independently reproduced.

scenarios.query_text: Was the validation cohort imputed using statistics learned from the development set, or was the imputer refit on combined data? Without a clear answer the validation AUC may be inflated by preprocessing leakage.

scenarios.query_text: Final predictors were retained based on p-value thresholds on a pre-specified shortlist. Why was an automated selection procedure (LASSO, stability selection, or boosted variable importance) over a broader candidate set not considered?

scenarios.description: Multi-omics OA risk subgroup models presented as sparse volcano plots rather than SHAP attributions, leaving reviewers unable to compare feature contributions across the four sibling models.
scenarios.query_text: Authors only show sparse volcano plots for three of the four subgroup risk models. The reader cannot tell which features actually drive each model. SHAP-style figures comparable across all models are needed for fair interpretability assessment.

scenarios.description: lncRNA-based prediction model lacks Shapley beeswarm plots that would communicate relative feature importance per transcript, blocking biological interpretation.
scenarios.query_text: The manuscript reports overall AUC for the lncRNA model but never plots per-feature contributions. A Shapley beeswarm summary would let readers judge which transcripts carry the predictive signal versus noise.

scenarios.description: ECG-based CAD model presents SHAP summaries but never maps them back to clinically meaningful waveform components or shows positive/negative case examples.
scenarios.query_text: The SHAP figures list ECG-derived features but never tie them back to QRS, ST or T-wave morphology that a cardiologist would recognise. Without paired positive and negative tracings the explainability claim is unfounded.

scenarios.description: Longitudinal plasma proteomics dementia predictor reports no post-hoc explainability outputs at all, making it impossible to identify which proteins drive risk scores.
scenarios.query_text: No SHAP, permutation importance, or other post-hoc tool is shown for the protein panel. Reviewers cannot evaluate whether the prediction is dominated by one obvious biomarker or by a coherent multi-protein signature.

scenarios.description: LASSO-selected protein panel never demonstrates that the same biomarkers persist under alternative selection algorithms, leaving feature stability unverified.
scenarios.query_text: Only LASSO was used to pick the final biomarker set. Did the same proteins survive under elastic net, stability selection, or Boruta? Without that comparison the panel may simply be a single algorithm's preference.

scenarios.description: Cohort prediction algorithm retains variables based purely on univariate p-value thresholds without any data-driven selection benchmark.
scenarios.query_text: Predictors were screened by univariable p-value before entering the multivariable model. This well-known shortcut introduces selection bias and overfits. Why was no penalised or data-driven approach tried on the broader candidate list?

scenarios.description: Diabetes phenotyping model fixes the final feature count at exactly ten without showing sensitivity to that hyperparameter choice.
scenarios.query_text: Why ten features and not five, fifteen, or twenty? The manuscript treats this as fixed but never reports performance curves across feature counts. The choice looks tuned for a target AUROC.

scenarios.description: Deep-learning prognosis model from tumour imaging is not shown to add information beyond tumour stage and size, so the explainability claim may collapse to a confounder.
scenarios.query_text: Stage alone is a powerful prognostic factor. The authors should show that the deep model's risk score remains predictive after adjusting for stage and tumour diameter, otherwise SHAP-style explanations are likely just re-encoding size.

scenarios.description: Multimodal lung cancer screening model produces attention heatmaps that highlight meaningless tokens such as family-history words and numerals, undermining the cross-modal interpretability claim.
scenarios.query_text: The attention overlay shows the model focusing on words like 'brother' or the digits '142'. That looks like spurious token attention. Please demonstrate that the imaging and text streams actually contribute complementary signal rather than the text branch latching onto artefacts.

scenarios.description: Lens-age deep learning model uses Grad-CAM to localise regions but cannot identify which lens pathologies (nuclear sclerosis vs cortical vs subcapsular) drive predictions.
scenarios.query_text: Grad-CAM tells us where the network looked but not what lens change it cared about. Without correlating attention to graded nuclear, cortical, or posterior subcapsular features, the LensAge biomarker cannot be interpreted clinically.

scenarios.description: GWAS-meta-analysis lifestyle prediction model is described as 'large scale' despite case counts insufficient to detect genome-wide significant variants.
scenarios.query_text: Labelling this as a large-scale GWAS overstates what the case count supports. With this many events the study is underpowered for genome-wide significance. Please temper the claim and report explicit power calculations for the SNP associations.

scenarios.description: Noninvasive CKD screening model has only 47 patients in the Somalia subgroup and very few MCD/FSGS cases, with no formal power calculation reported.
scenarios.query_text: The Somalia cohort has n=47 and the MCD/FSGS pathology subtypes are similarly tiny. Pooled AUROC hides this. Please show power calculations and subgroup-stratified performance so readers can judge generalisability across pathologies.

scenarios.description: Pregnancy cfRNA biomarker study has only 13-15 effective cases in the discovery cohort at 28wk, capping the multivariable model at two predictors and violating events-per-variable guidance.
scenarios.query_text: With roughly 13 cases at the 28-week timepoint, only two predictors can stably enter the model under standard EPV rules. The two-feature ceiling is a symptom of underpowering, not biology. Please discuss explicitly.

scenarios.description: Chinese T2D phenotyping pipeline uses a VAE without clarifying whether it functions as representation learning, feature selection, or denoising, nor comparing to simpler baselines.
scenarios.query_text: It is unclear what role the VAE actually plays. Is it doing representation learning, dimensionality reduction, or denoising? Without ablating against a vanilla autoencoder or PCA the added complexity is unjustified.

scenarios.description: CT-based COVID severity stratification model never documents when each scan was taken relative to admission, risking lead-time bias where late scans encode disease progression already realised.
scenarios.query_text: The risk model uses CT features but never states when in the hospitalisation the scan was acquired. If late scans are mixed in, the model may simply be seeing the progression it is asked to predict. Please document scan timing relative to the prediction anchor.

scenarios.description: Retracted Nature Human Behaviour fMRI paper (Just et al. 2017) — stepwise feature selection performed on the full dataset before LOOCV, with information from held-out subjects leaking into voxel-feature selection; identified by Verstynen and Kording's Matters Arising.
scenarios.query_text: Stepwise voxel selection appears to have been performed on the full dataset prior to the leave-one-out cross-validation, so that information from the supposedly held-out subject leaks into the feature ranking. With only a few dozen participants, the reported classifier accuracy is therefore tuned to this specific cohort rather than measuring genuine generalization to new individuals.
scenarios.ood_provenance: Retracted April 2023 (retraction DOI 10.1038/s41562-023-01581-1) after Verstynen & Kording (Matters Arising, 10.1038/s41562-023-01560-6) demonstrated stepwise feature selection caused information leakage between holdout and CV, inflating the reported 91% suicidality classifier accuracy.

scenarios.description: Yagis et al. 2021 (Sci Rep) — 2D CNN Alzheimer/Parkinson MRI classifiers split slices from the same subject across training and test folds; corrected subject-level split drops accuracy from ~94% to ~66%.
scenarios.query_text: The authors split the 3D MRI volumes by 2D slice rather than by subject, so different axial slices of the same patient end up in both the training and the held-out folds. This kind of slice-level partitioning is known to inflate Alzheimer's classification accuracy by roughly thirty points; a subject-level split is required before any of the reported performance numbers can be trusted.
scenarios.ood_provenance: Published Sci Rep critique quantifying inflation: slice-level CV achieved 94% AD accuracy on the same dataset where subject-level CV achieved only 66% (28-point gap). The paper is itself a critique of common practice in DL-for-AD literature.

Reported AUROC drops sharply when the model is applied to a genuinely external hospital, which is consistent with confounder-driven shortcut learning rather than learned disease signal.

Any classifier trained on this construction will primarily learn adult-versus-pediatric thoracic anatomy, which has nothing to do with COVID-19 detection.

The composite outcome also uses ICD-coded sepsis with SIRS plus organ dysfunction within six hours, which inflates apparent prediction by partially capturing already-manifest disease.

scenarios.description: JAMA Network Open 2025 — review of MIMIC-based AI models showed ~40% used discharge-finalized ICD codes (e.g., cardiac arrest, brain death, palliative-care encounter) as features in same-admission mortality prediction, reaching AUC ~0.98 via label leakage.
scenarios.query_text: The mortality model uses ICD codes such as cardiac arrest, brain death, and palliative-care encounter as input features, even though MIMIC documentation states ICD codes are assigned and finalized only after discharge. Predicting in-hospital mortality from codes that include events occurring at or after death is label leakage, and the reported AUROC near 0.98 reflects this rather than a clinically deployable real-time predictor.
scenarios.ood_provenance: JAMA Network Open 2025 systematic study: 37 of 92 MIMIC AI prediction studies used post-hoc ICD codes as features in same-admission outcome prediction. Companion editorial 'Avoiding Label Leakage in AI Risk Models—A Shared Responsibility' (jamanetworkopen.2025.43xxx) confirms this as a pervasive label-leakage failure.

scenarios.description: PLOS ONE 2021 radiomics methodology paper — showed that with small-sample radiomics, a single random train/test split produces wildly different AUROC across reseeds, and that performance gaps are 0.15-0.29 when feature selection precedes CV.
scenarios.query_text: A single random eighty-twenty split is used to report the headline AUROC on a modest radiomics cohort, with feature selection apparently run on the full dataset before cross-validation. Both choices are known to produce unstable and optimistically biased estimates; resplitting the cohort across many seeds and confining feature selection inside each CV fold typically erases most of the reported gap over baseline.
scenarios.ood_provenance: Demircioglu PLOS ONE 2021 quantified that single-split radiomics studies on small samples (n<200) give unreliable AUROC and overoptimistic results; combined with Insights into Imaging 2021 showing feature-selection-before-CV biases AUROC by up to 0.15. Both are widely cited methodological critiques of the radiomics literature.

As Roberts and colleagues showed across the COVID imaging literature, this combination of unverified patient-level isolation and absent external or prospective validation reliably produces optimistic but clinically unusable models.

scenarios.description: Springer Nature retracted ~40 papers (Dec 2025, via Retraction Watch / The Transmitter) that trained CNNs to classify autism from children's face photos scraped from autism-related websites, with no diagnostic confirmation, no consent, and obvious confounds.
scenarios.query_text: The training corpus is roughly 3,000 children's photographs scraped from autism-advocacy websites and re-uploaded to a Kaggle dataset, with no clinical diagnostic confirmation, no parental consent, and no standardized acquisition. Without verified ASD status, controlled lighting and pose, or any external validation cohort, the model cannot be claimed to detect autism rather than dataset provenance, photographer style, or pose differences.

scenarios.description: ICU benchmark framework that only supports a narrow set of 52 numeric vital/lab features and ignores diagnoses, prescriptions, clinical notes, and imaging that are widely available in MIMIC/eICU, masking the genuine ceiling that richer-feature models could reach.
scenarios.query_text: Although the benchmark covers a number of ICU datasets, it ingests only about 52 features that are mostly vital signs and lab values, and it discards diagnoses, prescriptions, clinical notes, and imaging that those source databases actually contain. This narrow feature panel may explain why the deep and classical baselines look almost indistinguishable in the reported tables, and it limits how much future modelling work can extract from the framework.

scenarios.description: Multi-cohort ICU benchmark that omits basic per-dataset statistics (patient counts, ICU stays, outcome prevalence) from the main text, leaving readers unable to tell whether pooled training is dominated by a single dataset or whether prevalence differences are driving the cross-cohort performance gaps in the headline figure.
scenarios.query_text: Basic dataset statistics such as the number of patients, the number of ICU stays, and the outcome prevalence per cohort are missing from the main paper and only appear in the appendix. Without them, it is impossible to tell whether the apparent performance differences across cohorts in the main figure are simply driven by prevalence shifts, and whether the pooled training set is dominated by one source database.
scenarios.ood_provenance: ICLR 2024 — Yet Another ICU Benchmark — Reviewer oWMD flagged missing per-cohort prevalence/statistics in the main text

scenarios.description: Medical VLM reliability benchmark consisting of only 352 visually confusing image pairs sourced from a single dataset (ROCO), so any reported failure rates may not transfer to broader modalities (ultrasound, nuclear medicine) or anatomic regions.
scenarios.query_text: The benchmark is rigorous but only contains 352 questions across 9 categories drawn from one source dataset (ROCO). At this scale it cannot capture the full spectrum of medical image complexity, and the conclusion that models fall below random guessing might not transfer to ultrasound, nuclear medicine, or other modalities and anatomic regions that were never tested.
scenarios.ood_provenance: ICLR 2025 — MediConfusion — Reviewer QM8Q raised tiny dataset size + single-source coverage

scenarios.description: VLM benchmark where every evaluated model scores below random chance on the test pairs, but the authors do not probe whether the failure mode is genuine inability to distinguish image pairs or an artefact of the similarity thresholds used to construct pairs, leaving the headline claim of unreliability unsupported by mechanism.
scenarios.query_text: All open and closed source models perform below random guessing on this benchmark, but the paper does not investigate why. Varying the medical and generic similarity thresholds used to build the confusing pairs and comparing model scores would tell us whether the models cannot differentiate any pair at all, or just fail on the hardest ones, and that mechanism is missing from the analysis.
scenarios.ood_provenance: ICLR 2025 — MediConfusion — Reviewer cT2V questioned the rationale for below-random performance without threshold sensitivity

scenarios.query_text: On the MIMIC-III mortality prediction task the positive rate is only 5.42%, which means a trivial 'always survive' predictor already reaches about 94.6% accuracy. Reporting accuracy in this setting is not informative, and the headline gains are difficult to interpret without AUROC and AUPRC, which are standard for imbalanced clinical outcomes.

Given that the improvement over the closest GraphRAG-style baseline is small, the reader has no way to judge whether the gains are real or within run-to-run noise.

scenarios.description: Patient-clinical-journey LLM benchmark that scores model responses almost entirely with automated text-overlap metrics (BLEU, etc.) and lacks clinician-rated qualitative review of clinical correctness, so a higher BLEU score does not translate into a defensible claim about clinical safety or utility.
scenarios.query_text: Evaluation across the patient-journey tasks relies heavily on automated metrics like BLEU, which capture surface text overlap but not whether the generated answer is clinically appropriate or safe. Without qualitative scoring by clinical experts on a sample of outputs, the benchmark cannot support claims about real-world utility, and a higher BLEU score does not establish that an LLM should be trusted in any of the four care stages.
scenarios.ood_provenance: NeurIPS 2024 D&B — MedJourney — Reviewer G1cc raised BLEU-only evaluation without clinical expert assessment

scenarios.query_text: The paper does not publish the criteria used to pick which diseases, which scenarios, and which datasets enter the benchmark, so we cannot tell how representative it is of rare diseases or genuinely complex clinical situations. Without that transparency the claim that the benchmark mirrors a real patient journey is hard to accept, and the model rankings could easily be a function of the cases the authors happened to include.

scenarios.description: TRIPOD+AI item 19 critique: many published prediction-model papers report only discrimination (AUROC) and place calibration plots in the supplement or omit them entirely. scenarios.query_text: The authors report only the AUROC on the held-out test set and provide no calibration plot, no calibration-in-the-large, no calibration slope, and no Hosmer-Lemeshow-type assessment in the main text. TRIPOD+AI explicitly requires that calibration be evaluated and reported because a discriminating but miscalibrated model can over- or under-estimate risk at the operating point used clinically.
scenarios.ood_provenance: TRIPOD+AI 2024 statement, items 19a/19b (Calibration). Same failure mode as the Wong 2021 Michigan Epic Sepsis Model external validation, which found inadequate calibration alongside low AUROC.

scenarios.query_text: The label used for training and evaluation is a downstream administrative surrogate (hospital admission for severe respiratory illness) rather than a directly adjudicated case of the target condition. PROBAST+AI and the Wynants systematic review flag this kind of proxy-outcome substitution as a high-risk-of-bias outcome-domain problem because the model is really being trained to predict resource-use patterns, not the disease itself.

scenarios.description: Roberts et al. (2021 Nat Mach Intell) flagged the widespread practice of building COVID-19 chest-imaging classifiers by combining adult COVID-positive X-rays from one public repository with non-COVID pediatric pneumonia X-rays from another. The model then learns age and acquisition protocol, not disease.
scenarios.query_text: The COVID-positive images and the non-COVID control images appear to come from entirely different source repositories and patient populations (in particular, the negatives include a pediatric pneumonia public set while the positives are adult). A classifier built this way is almost certainly learning age, acquisition device, and source-of-data rather than COVID-19 imaging features, which Roberts and colleagues have shown is the single most common methodological failure in this literature.
scenarios.ood_provenance: Roberts et al. 2021 NMI flagged dozens of COVID-19 imaging models for case-vs-control source mismatch (e.g., adult COVID positives paired with pediatric pneumonia negatives from Kermany/Mooney datasets). None of those flagged COVID-imaging papers are in peer-review-kb.json.

scenarios.description: DeGrave et al. (2021 NMI) demonstrated that high-performing COVID-19 chest-X-ray models latched onto laterality tokens, hospital text overlays, and image-border artifacts; saliency maps placed importance on background pixels rather than lung fields.
scenarios.query_text: When the saliency maps for the top-performing model are inspected, the salient pixels lie outside the lung parenchyma, on burn-in text and laterality markers. DeGrave and colleagues have shown that this pattern of attention to non-anatomical artifacts is diagnostic of shortcut learning, and the headline AUROC therefore cannot be interpreted as evidence the model has learned COVID-19 pathology.
scenarios.ood_provenance: DeGrave 2021 Nature Machine Intelligence shortcut-learning analysis of three high-profile published COVID-CXR models; none of the analysed models are in peer-review-kb.json.

scenarios.description: Zech et al. (2018 PLOS Medicine) showed that a pneumonia CNN trained on NIH+Mount Sinai performed worse externally because it had learned to identify hospital system and within-hospital department, both of which correlate strongly with disease prevalence.
scenarios.query_text: Headline performance was estimated on a held-out set drawn from the same two hospital systems used for training. The Zech 2018 PLOS Medicine study showed that CNNs can effectively learn hospital-of-origin as a proxy for disease prevalence, so in-distribution test AUROC will be optimistic and a truly external multi-site validation is mandatory before any deployment claim.
scenarios.ood_provenance: Zech 2018 PLOS Medicine pneumonia generalization study, cited as the canonical example of hospital-system confounding in TRIPOD+AI/PROBAST+AI applicability discussions. Not in peer-review-kb.json.

scenarios.query_text: Reported development-cohort AUROC values come exclusively from the developer's own multi-site retrospective dataset. The Wong 2021 Michigan external validation of the Epic Sepsis Model showed a discrimination drop from 0.76-0.83 to 0.63, a sensitivity of only 33%, and an alert rate of 18% of admissions. Until an independent external validation is performed, the vendor performance cannot be trusted for deployment claims.

scenarios.description: Riley 2020 BMJ argued that the EPV>=10 heuristic is inadequate; correct minimum sample size for binary outcomes should be computed from expected R-squared, target shrinkage, and outcome prevalence. The Riley criteria apply to ML and not only to regression. Most published ML prediction-model papers do not meet the Riley minimum.
scenarios.query_text: With roughly 180 events distributed across more than 40 candidate predictors fed into XGBoost and a multilayer perceptron, the development cohort is well below the Riley 2020 minimum sample size for a multivariable prediction model. The authors provide no formal pmsampsize-style calculation and rely implicitly on the obsolete 10-EPV rule of thumb, so optimism and overfitting are essentially guaranteed.
scenarios.ood_provenance: Riley 2020 BMJ minimum-sample-size paper plus Riley 2023 Biometrical Journal stability paper; cited in TRIPOD+AI item 8 / PROBAST+AI analysis domain. The Riley papers and the systematic-review evidence of EPV violations are not in peer-review-kb.json.

scenarios.description: Maguire/Oakden-Rayner and others critiqued Rajpurkar et al.'s CheXNet (2017 arXiv) for comparing the algorithm to radiologists who were denied prior imaging, clinical history, and lateral views, i.e. judging humans at the low end of their performance envelope while the algorithm was trained on the in-distribution NIH labels.
scenarios.query_text: Radiologists in the head-to-head comparison were given only single frontal chest X-rays with no prior studies, no lateral view, and no clinical history, while the algorithm was tuned on labels generated by an automated NLP pipeline over the same NIH dataset. This kind of asymmetric reader-study design measures the low-end of human performance and inflates the apparent superiority of the model, a critique levelled at CheXNet and its successors.
scenarios.ood_provenance: Lauren Oakden-Rayner's CheXNet critique plus the broader STARD-AI/DECIDE-AI discussion of reader-study design. CheXNet (arXiv:1711.05225) is not in peer-review-kb.json.

scenarios.query_text: The headline framing is that a gradient-boosted ensemble beats traditional regression, but no penalized logistic regression baseline is reported with the same predictors, the same preprocessing, and the same train/test split. Christodoulou and colleagues showed that in low-risk-of-bias comparisons logistic regression generally matches modern ML on tabular clinical data; without that baseline the claimed ML advantage cannot be evaluated.
scenarios.ood_provenance: Christodoulou, Steyerberg, Van Calster et al. 2019 systematic review (J Clin Epidemiol); endorsed in TRIPOD+AI item 12 (model development methods). Not in peer-review-kb.json.

The evaluation should be driven by the false negative rate and the false omission rate, because a missed positive in early breast cancer detection has real clinical consequences and the high headline accuracy may simply reflect imbalance rather than true detection ability.

ROC, calibration plots and precision-recall curves are missing, and the clinical-deployment readiness conclusions are overstated without independent validation on a real hospital cohort.
